summary: Explores issues in defining a standard for exchanging mathematical equations between systems. It does not attempt a full definition, and asks more questions than it answers. User interface questions are addressed only where they affect interchange.

eli5.summary: Writing math on a computer is hard to share, because different programs draw it differently. This memo asks what we would need to agree on so everyone could swap equations.

questions: how to exchange mathematical equations between computers
what are the issues in an equation representation standard
what are the issues in defining an equations standard
subtitle: A discussion of what a standard for exchanging mathematical equations should represent.

tldr.problem: Scientists want to include mathematical equations in electronic mail, but there is no standard format. Different equation systems (LaTeX, EQN, VIEWPOINT) use incompatible representations, making it impossible to exchange equations reliably between users of different systems.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC examines existing equation systems (directive systems like EQN, full display systems like Xerox STAR, and symbolic systems like Macsyma) and argues for a standard similar to EQN but with extensions. The standard should represent mathematical symbols and their positions, support common constructs like subscripts and fractions without specifying exact positions, and allow positioning of symbols anywhere when needed.
tldr.outcome: The RFC poses more questions than it answers, serving as a call for the community to begin defining an equations standard. It identifies key design choices and tradeoffs but leaves the detailed specification to future work.

today: RFC 1003 raises important questions about equation representation that remain relevant. While no single standard emerged from this RFC, the landscape evolved through multiple approaches. MathML (for XML) and LaTeX became widely used for equation interchange, though the broader question of a universal equation standard that serves all user communities remains partly unresolved.

sections.title: Why Equations in Electronic Mail Matter
sections.content:
Electronic mail has become an essential tool for researchers. With the NSF supercomputer initiative bringing many scientists online who are not yet accustomed to email, there will soon be a much larger scientific community using email.

Unlike computer scientists and engineers, many scientists communicate heavily through equations. A glance through any scientific journal shows that mathematics dominates many fields. When these scientists get email, they will expect to be able to include equations in their messages, just as they would in a printed paper.

Currently, there is no standard for representing equations. Some users propose including source files from their own equation system (like LaTeX or EQN), but this is not a good long-term solution because different systems are incompatible. The time is right to define a standard that meets both present and future needs.
sections.eli5: Soon, many scientists will be using email for the first time. They will want to send each other math problems and answers. But different computers use different ways to write math, so people can't understand each other's equations.

sections.title: Existing Equation Systems
sections.content:
The RFC surveys three main types of equation systems in use:

Directive systems like LaTeX and EQN represent equations as text with special commands. For example, EQN uses directives like over for fractions and sup for superscripts. These are easy to transfer as plain text in email. Users can edit them with standard text editors. However, they require understanding the syntax, which is difficult for non-programmers and professional typesetters.

Full display systems like Xerox STAR and VIEWPOINT let users type or point to create equations while seeing them rendered on screen. However, they are specific to particular hardware and store equations in proprietary internal formats. The systems have limitations; for example, VIEWPOINT cannot place all symbols arbitrarily.

Symbolic systems like Macsyma and Reduce also handle equations, but they represent mathematical meaning rather than displayed appearance. They are useful for computation but are too restrictive for general mathematical communication.
sections.eli5: There are three kinds of systems: ones where you type commands (like programming), ones where you draw (WYSIWYG), and ones that understand math. Each has advantages and problems.

sections.title: What Should Be Represented
sections.content:
The RFC identifies a spectrum of representation levels. At one end, you could store a bitmap of the printed equation (inefficient). At the other end, you could represent the mathematical meaning (too restrictive). In between are several possibilities:

Characters and fonts only: Store symbols and fonts, allowing any symbol anywhere (like Interleaf's system). This is general but requires the user to position everything manually.

Discrete positions: Allow symbols only at discrete grid positions (like Hockney's Egg on the IBM PC). This makes subscripts and superscripts easier to align.

Structured format: Use a language that understands mathematical structures like subscripts, fractions, and matrices. Positioning is automatic but can be overridden (like EQN or LaTeX).

System language: Translate to the native format of a system like Troff or TeX.

The RFC argues for a combination: a structured format like EQN with extensions to allow absolute positioning when needed. This gives compact representation for common cases while allowing exceptions.
sections.eli5: You could store the picture as a bitmap (wastes space), as individual letters with positions (hard to use), as structured math (easy to type, works well), or as code (very compact). A good standard would use structured math most of the time but allow individual positioning when needed.

sections.title: A Proposed Standard Design
sections.content:
The RFC proposes that a standard should have these characteristics:

Compatibility: It should be able to represent equations from existing systems. Directive systems should map almost directly into it. Full display systems should be translatable into it.

Simplicity for common cases: Standard mathematical symbols and all Greek and Latin letters should be available. Common constructs like subscripts, superscripts, fractions, matrices, and growing parentheses should be easy to express without specifying exact positions.

Flexibility for special cases: When positioning needs to be exact, the standard should allow specifying absolute coordinates. This handles exceptions without making the common case complex.

Text representation: The standard should use ordinary text that can be sent in email messages. This lets directive systems map to it easily and lets full display systems output it (perhaps with lots of absolute positioning).

User interface independence: Typesetting knowledge should be in programs and user interfaces, not required of users. Different user interfaces—directive editors for programmers and WYSIWYG for non-specialists—should be possible.
sections.eli5: The standard should: work like EQN, handle common things easily, allow placing anything anywhere if needed, be text that can go in email, and let different programs use different ways to let people type equations.

sections.title: Open Questions and Next Steps
sections.content:
The RFC identifies key questions that need to be resolved:

Should the standard be biased toward directive systems (text-based) or full display systems (point-and-click)? The RFC suggests directive systems are better for specialists but full display systems work better for non-specialists.

What level of structural knowledge should the standard assume? Should it understand fractions, matrices, and growing parentheses, or should these be optional extensions?

How should the standard handle the distinction between the display of an equation and its mathematical meaning? The RFC argues these are separate concerns and the standard should focus on display, not mathematical semantics.

How should the standard be extended over time without breaking compatibility with existing equations?

The RFC makes clear that this is a starting point for discussion. Implementation experience and feedback from the NSF user community will guide the eventual standard. The goal is to enable scientists to exchange equations via email just as easily as they exchange text.
sections.eli5: The RFC asks: should the format be for typing or for pointing? Should it understand math structures? Should it be about how it looks or what it means? And how do we let it grow without breaking old equations? These are the questions the community needs to answer.
